p.docTitle: Report of the Plenary of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services on the work of its eleventh session

division.heading: Opening of the session

content.p: The eleventh session of the Plenary of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) was held at the Mercure Hotel, Windhoek, from 10 to 16 December 2024.
Following a musical performance and a video presentation outlining the many achievements of IPBES, the session was opened at 10 a.m. by the Chair of IPBES, David Obura, who welcomed participants.

Opening statements were delivered by Anne Larigauderie, IPBES Executive Secretary; António de Sousa Abreu, Director of the Division of Ecological and Earth Sciences, United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), speaking on behalf of the four United Nations organizations supporting IPBES, namely the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and UNESCO; Astrid Schomaker, Executive Secretary, Convention on Biological Diversity; Pohamba Shifeta, Minister of Environment, Forestry and Tourism, Namibia; and the Chair of IPBES.

In her statement, Ms. Larigauderie welcomed participants and expressed her gratitude to Mr. Shifeta for attending the session, to the Government of Namibia for hosting the session, and to the other institutions and individuals involved for their efforts and dedication in preparing for it. She expressed great satisfaction that the current IPBES session was the first to be held in Africa and the first to be chaired by a person from Africa. She recalled notable activities and developments since the tenth session, including the efforts to produce several critically important reports that would be instrumental in informing the implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. Those reports included the two assessments to be considered at the current session: the thematic assessment of the interlinkages among biodiversity, water, food and health (nexus assessment) and the thematic assessment of the underlying causes of biodiversity loss and the determinants of transformative change and options for achieving the 2050 Vision for Biodiversity (transformative change assessment). She noted that the previously approved assessments, including the one on invasive alien species, continued to have an impact, and that the IPBES impact-tracking database (TRACK) now had several hundred examples of specific impacts at many different scales. In addition, IPBES had been awarded the very prestigious Blue Planet Prize for its work at the interface between science and policy, a sign of great recognition of the value and impact of the work of the Platform and the entire IPBES community. The Platform had continued to grow since the tenth session and now had 147 members, some 60 per cent more than in 2012, when it had been launched. A total of 850 participants had registered to attend the current session, including representatives from more than 130 Governments, and the stakeholders’ day preceding the session had been attended by more than 400 participants.

In closing, Ms. Larigauderie thanked everyone who had contributed to IPBES over the past year, including its members, stakeholders and the more than 800 experts who had volunteered their time for the work of the Platform. She also thanked the Government of Germany for its unwavering support in hosting the IPBES secretariat. Noting that the current Plenary session would be her last as Executive Secretary, she wished everyone successful deliberations and an inspiring session.

In his statement, Mr. Abreu recalled that the global community had taken significant strides in addressing the biodiversity crisis and that the IPBES assessments had been instrumental in those advancements, as they had informed negotiations with a baseline of knowledge, highlighted the importance of a whole-of-society approach to responding to the planetary crises and recognized the role of Indigenous stewardship in the conservation and sustainable use of nature and biodiversity. The four United Nations organizations were committed to supporting States in implementing the Convention on Biological Diversity and the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. In that regard, he expressed satisfaction that nine new projects, in which all four organizations were involved, had been approved under the new Kunming Biodiversity Fund. The nexus and transformative change assessments would help countries to navigate their journey towards a world living in harmony with nature and would guide many of their concrete actions.

Outlining the organizations’ commitment to supporting IPBES and its mission, he said that UNEP was proud to host the secretariat of IPBES and to provide technical support through the World Conservation Monitoring Centre. Through its National Ecosystem Assessment Initiative, UNEP, in cooperation with UNDP and UNESCO, supported States in undertaking national ecosystem assessments based on the IPBES conceptual framework and assessment process. FAO contributed to the IPBES programme of work and provided updates to its own governing bodies on the IPBES assessments to inform decision-making and technical programming. Through an extensive network of projects and programmes, UNDP continued to champion the uptake of IPBES assessments, including through the Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services Network. UNESCO was committed to safeguarding the world’s interlinked cultural and natural heritage through mechanisms such as the Man and the Biosphere Programme, the Convention for the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage, the Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage and the World Network of Biosphere Reserves.

In closing, he said that robust collective action was essential to tackle the interconnected crises of biodiversity loss, climate change and environmental degradation. The work of IPBES was more critical than ever in bridging science and policy to provide the knowledge and tools required to drive the transformation, change and benefits that planet Earth and nature needed.

In her opening remarks, Ms. Schomaker noted with appreciation that the groundbreaking and seminal work of IPBES had paved the way for the adoption of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. IPBES provided the knowledge required by the secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity in order to ground its work in robust evidence on biodiversity as well as its interaction with socioeconomic systems. She expressed appreciation to the Chair of IPBES for ensuring that the voice of science had been clear and that its messages had been persuasive at the sixteenth meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity, held in Cali, Colombia, at which a number of important decisions had been adopted. In those decisions and in the related deliberations, the parties had frequently made reference to the work of IPBES and had proposed five new topics for future assessments under the IPBES rolling programme of work. She noted that a sense of urgency commensurate with the crisis afflicting the planet still seemed to be missing and that IPBES could again play a crucial role in ensuring that parties had access to up-to-date, relevant and sound science. She expressed confidence that the nexus and transformative change assessments would make a significant contribution to closing the remaining gap between existing policies and those that were needed.

Highlighting the long history of cooperation between the secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity and IPBES, she pledged that the Convention secretariat would continue to work in partnership with IPBES to support national action and to explore all avenues for closer cooperation. The much-anticipated second global assessment would have to deliver on a number of crucial aspects, meaning that the scoping exercise at the current session was of critical importance. In addition, the monitoring assessment to be considered for finalization by the Plenary of IPBES at its thirteenth session would also be highly relevant at the seventeenth meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity. In closing, she emphasized that acceleration was the order of the day and that a global surge in implementation was urgently needed. The international community could rely on IPBES and on science as allies in achieving the goals and targets of the Global Biodiversity Framework.

Welcoming participants, Mr. Shifeta noted that their presence reflected the collective commitment of countries to address the pressing global challenges of biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation. The two landmark reports under consideration at the current session epitomized the purpose of IPBES as a platform that bridged science, policy and action. As the first African country to have enshrined environmental protection in its Constitution, Namibia had been unwavering in its commitment to biodiversity and the conservation of ecosystems, which were conserved and maintained through State-protected areas, communal conservancies and privately owned and managed conservation areas. Those areas provided biodiversity and ecosystem protection across more than 40 per cent of the country’s land mass, already exceeding target 3 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (to conserve 30 per cent of the world’s land, waters and seas by 2030).

The remarkable conservation success of Namibia was accompanied by the challenge of human-wildlife conflict, which posed significant risks to vulnerable communities. He encouraged participants to seek collaborative strategies in order to balance biodiversity conservation, policy formulation and science with the well-being of communities. Namibia and other countries in Southern Africa recognized the critical role of trophy hunting in conservation and sustainable development. In conjunction with community-based conservation models, such hunting, known as "conservation hunting" in his country, could contribute significantly to the protection of biodiversity and ecosystems, with the revenue generated not only benefiting rural communities directly, but also supporting anti-poaching initiatives and wildlife conservation efforts.

Noting that the findings of the nexus and transformative change assessments highlighted the urgent need for integrated, cross-sectoral approaches, he called on all stakeholders to strengthen international cooperation, to increase financial and technical support for biodiversity-rich nations and to prioritize the inclusion of local communities in conservation strategies, with due consideration of the disproportionate burden of climate change borne by Africa. He encouraged participants to reflect on the transformative potential of the discussions at the current session, to acknowledge the need to implement solutions with urgency and determination, to recognize the diversity of representatives and their perspectives, and to bear in mind the collective responsibility to preserve the natural world for future generations. He thanked the generous donors, whose support had been instrumental in making IPBES a reality, and, on behalf of the Government and people of Namibia, he expressed his deepest appreciation to all participants for their contributions to the Platform.

In his opening remarks, the Chair said that, over the past decade, the Platform had enjoyed a number of successes, for example, sharing the Gulbenkian Prize for Humanity in 2022 and being awarded the Blue Planet Prize in 2024. Such accolades were recognition of the credibility of the Platform’s assessments, the work of its task forces and the importance of the integration of science and knowledge, including Indigenous knowledge, for decision-making at various levels. The Platform’s work had also contributed to the efforts of those working to put policy into action and to further science and knowledge. At a time when multilateral processes were facing significant issues, and the challenges to nature and humanity were intensifying and interacting, it was more important than ever to maintain the Platform’s reputation and integrity.

The current session came at a pivotal moment: the Plenary could lead the international community into 2025 and the last five years of the Sustainable Development Goals, the 2030 targets of the Convention on Biological Diversity and other related policy processes with 2030 milestones. At the current session, the Plenary would consider two assessments that were of vital importance to the global crises. The first assessment delved deeply into those challenges; the elements it covered represented a microcosm of the complexity and variety of life lived on the shared planet Earth. The second assessment sought to explore sustainable scenarios for the future and contained exhaustive evidence on the barriers and obstacles to transformative change, while also identifying the ingredients of positive change that would help stakeholders in their efforts to live in harmony with nature. The Plenary would also set the course for the Platform’s second global assessment of biodiversity and ecosystem services, as well as explore new ways of working with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) on climate change and biodiversity loss. In closing, he thanked the Government of Namibia for hosting the current session and said that he looked forward to working to find common ground to facilitate global efforts towards sustainable pathways for the future and to reaffirm the relevance of the Platform’s work.

The representatives of Mauritania on behalf of the Group of African States; Pakistan on behalf of the Group of Asia-Pacific States; Bosnia and Herzegovina on behalf of the Group of Eastern European States; Mexico on behalf of the Group of Latin American and Caribbean States; Hungary on behalf of the European Union and its member States; and the United States of America, speaking also on behalf of Japan, Canada, Australia, Norway and New Zealand, made general statements in which they spoke of the progress of IPBES to date, applauded the Platform for being awarded the Blue Planet Prize, highlighted the challenges faced and activities carried out in support of IPBES of those for whom they spoke, commended the work of the experts on the assessments to be considered by the Plenary and outlined their expectations for the current session and the future work of IPBES. The representatives of two stakeholders – the Open-ended Network of IPBES Stakeholders and the International Indigenous Forum on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services – also delivered statements.
The Chair announced that the Bureau had elected Hamid Čustović (Bosnia and Herzegovina) to serve as Rapporteur of the eleventh session.

intro.p: Assessing knowledge:

content.p: Thematic assessment of the interlinkages among biodiversity, water, food and health;
Thematic assessment of the underlying causes of biodiversity loss and the determinants of transformative change and options for achieving the 2050 Vision for Biodiversity;
Scoping report for a second global assessment of biodiversity and ecosystem services;
Engagement with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.
Building capacity, strengthening knowledge foundations and supporting policy.
Improving the effectiveness of the Platform.
Organization of the Plenary; dates and venues of future sessions of the Plenary.
Institutional arrangements: United Nations collaborative partnership arrangement for the work of the Platform and its secretariat.
Adoption of the decisions and the report of the session.
Closure of the session.

The Plenary agreed to follow the organization of work set out in annex I to document IPBES/11/1/Add.1. The Plenary also agreed to establish two working groups. Working group I would consider agenda item 7 (a), on the thematic assessment of the interlinkages among biodiversity, water, food and health; item 7 (c), on a scoping report for a second global assessment of biodiversity and ecosystem services; and item 9, on improving the effectiveness of the Platform. Working group II would consider item 7 (b), on the thematic assessment of the underlying causes of biodiversity loss and the determinants of transformative change and options for achieving the 2050 Vision for Biodiversity; item 7 (d), on engagement with IPCC; and item 8, on building capacity, strengthening knowledge foundations and supporting policy. Each working group would consider in detail the summary for policymakers based on the chapters of the corresponding assessment, with a view to having both summaries for policymakers approved by the Plenary, and the chapters of the assessments accepted, without further discussion. Following its previous practice, the Plenary also agreed to assign consideration of agenda item 6, on financial and budgetary arrangements for the Platform, to a contact group.

One representative, emphasizing the need to ensure that the decisions and assessments adopted by the Platform benefited from the highest level of legitimacy, transparency and inclusivity, said that his delegation was deeply concerned that the heavy workload at the current session might place a disproportionate burden on small delegations, particularly those from developing countries. As his delegation comprised only one member, it would need to prioritize participation in one working group over the other. He expressed the hope that the Co-Chairs of working group II would therefore take his delegation’s written comments into consideration; his delegation nevertheless reserved the right to reopen in plenary the documents considered by working group II.

Subsequently, in the light of the heavy workload faced by working group I, the Plenary decided to reassign agenda item 9 from working group I to working group II in order to allow working group I to focus on item 7 (c).

subdivision.heading: Election of officers

content.p: Introducing the item, the Chair recalled that, at its tenth session, held in Bonn, Germany, from 28 August to 2 September 2023, the Plenary had elected 10 members to the Bureau. In accordance with the rules of procedure, those members would serve for a term of office that would end at the close of the thirteenth session of the Plenary.

In September 2024, a Bureau member from the Latin American and Caribbean States had resigned from the Bureau. In accordance with rule 22 of the rules of procedure, the secretariat had invited Governments from the Latin American and Caribbean States to submit to the secretariat proposals for candidates and accompanying curricula vitae by 15 November 2024. Governments from the region had also been invited to propose, by the same date, candidates to serve as alternate members of the Bureau. The names and curricula vitae of the candidates whose nominations had been received before 15 November 2024 had been made available in document IPBES/11/INF/25.
The Plenary elected the following members of the Bureau:

p.i: From Latin American and Caribbean States:

content.p: Bureau member: Hesiquio Benítez Díaz (Mexico)
Alternates: Ruleo Camacho (Antigua and Barbuda) and Paulina Stowhas (Chile)

The Chair congratulated the newly elected officers, who would serve for the remainder of the term of the present Bureau, until the election of their successors at the thirteenth session of the Platform.

division.heading: Admission of observers

content.p: Introducing the item, the Chair recalled that, at its tenth session, the Plenary had decided that the interim procedure for the admission of observers to sessions of the Plenary, as described in paragraph 22 of the report of the first session of the Plenary (IPBES/1/12) and applied at its second to tenth sessions, would be applied at its eleventh session. In accordance with that interim procedure, the observers admitted to the previous sessions of the Plenary, as listed in part I of the annex to document IPBES/11/INF/3, were among those admitted to the current session. Part II of that annex contained a list of 15 organizations recommended by the Bureau for admission as new observers to the current session of the Plenary, while part III contained a list of 3 applications not recommended for admission. The Plenary agreed to welcome the new observers, as recommended by the Bureau, to the eleventh session of the Plenary.

The Chair also recalled that, at previous sessions of the Plenary, diverging opinions had been expressed regarding the procedure for the admission of observers, as contained in paragraphs 14 to 17 of the draft policy and procedures for the admission of observers set out in the annex to document IPBES/11/2.

As positions on the matter had not changed, the Plenary decided that the Plenary, at its twelfth session, would continue to use the interim procedure for the admission of observers to sessions of the Plenary, as described in paragraph 22 of the report of the first session of the Plenary and applied at its second to eleventh sessions, on the understanding that observers admitted to its first to eleventh sessions would be among those admitted to its twelfth session.

division.heading: Report of the Executive Secretary on progress in the implementation of the rolling work programme up to 2030

content.p: Introducing the item, the Chair recalled that, in its decision IPBES-7/1, the Plenary had adopted the rolling work programme of IPBES for the period up to 2030. In its decision IPBES-10/1, it had requested the Executive Secretary to provide a report on progress in the implementation of the work programme to the Plenary at its eleventh session. The Executive Secretary, in consultation with the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel and the Bureau, had developed, for consideration by the Plenary, a report on progress in the implementation of the rolling work programme up to 2030 (IPBES/11/3). Additional information was set out in documents IPBES/11/INF/4 on the institutional arrangements established for the provision of technical support for the implementation of the work programme; IPBES/11/INF/8 on progress in the preparation of the business and biodiversity assessment and a fast-track methodological assessment on monitoring biodiversity and nature’s contributions to people; IPBES/11/INF/9 on the guide on the production of assessments; IPBES/11/INF/11 on the implementation of the conflict-of-interest policy; IPBES/11/INF/19 on strengthened communication; and IPBES/11/INF/20 on strengthened engagement of stakeholders.

The Executive Secretary presented her report on progress in the implementation of the rolling work programme up to 2030 according to its six objectives, with another representative of the secretariat outlining communication activities. The Executive Secretary also gave a brief overview of the staffing situation within the secretariat and the implementation of the conflict-of-interest policy.

Co-Chairs of the business and biodiversity assessment and the fast-track methodological assessment on monitoring biodiversity and nature’s contributions to people (monitoring assessment) delivered presentations on the development and implementation of those assessments. Each presentation provided information on the context and scope of the assessment; the team involved in work on the assessment; the structure of the assessment; progress made to date; and the steps and timeline for the completion of the assessment and consideration by the Plenary.

Several representatives expressed appreciation for the Executive Secretary’s report, the progress made on the rolling work programme since the tenth session and the commitment and dedication of the IPBES members, experts and stakeholders that had enabled that progress. One representative noted with appreciation that the mid-term review of the 2030 rolling programme would continue between the eleventh and twelfth session, underscoring that internal and external reviews helped to ensure transparency, foster continuous improvement and enhance the efficiency of the Platform. Another representative, while applauding the positive feedback from the media on the secretariat’s communication and engagement work, urged the secretariat to also solicit countries’ feedback on the ways in which they had benefited from the assessments.

A number of representatives noted that a significant amount of information had already been generated by work on the monitoring assessment and encouraged the sharing of that information with the secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity in advance of the resumed sixteenth meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention, where the monitoring framework for the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework would be an important topic of discussion.

One representative recommended that, given the tenor of the discussion on the summary for policymakers of the nexus assessment at the current session, the overall discussion methodology be given serious consideration, particularly as the future discussion on the business and biodiversity assessment promised to be complex and would touch on aspects affecting the interests of various countries.

Another representative suggested that, following her retirement as Executive Secretary, Ms. Larigauderie be appointed honorary ambassador of IPBES, with the mandate to meet with decision makers and disseminate the knowledge generated by the completed assessments.
The Plenary took note of the information provided and welcomed the work undertaken.

division.heading: Financial and budgetary arrangements for the Platform

content.p: In accordance with decision IPBES-10/3, the Executive Secretary provided an overview of the financial and budgetary arrangements for the Platform, as set out in the note by the secretariat on the matter (IPBES/11/4) and the note by the secretariat on the detailed cost of the implementation of the work programme (IPBES/11/INF/12). The total contributions and pledges received for 2023 amounted to around $7.9 million, from 21 Governments, the European Union and four other donors. Additional pledges and contributions for 2024 had been received since the documents had been issued, and the total contributions and pledges received to date for 2024 now stood at $5.8 million.

The Chair expressed appreciation to the countries and private sector donors that had contributed to the trust fund of the Platform and to the countries and organizations that had provided in-kind or other forms of support to IPBES. He also expressed gratitude to the hundreds of experts around the world who had devoted their time, free of charge, to the work of the Platform, thereby enabling IPBES to accomplish its mission and produce a great deal of work in a short amount of time, while making efficient use of its financial resources. Noting that there was nevertheless an urgent need for additional national contributions for 2024 and subsequent years in order to bridge the $2 million gap between the Platform’s average annual income and expenditure, he invited those Governments that had not yet done so to make pledges for 2024 and 2025.

In response, several representatives provided information on their countries’ contributions. The representative of the Kingdom of the Netherlands announced that his Government, which was committed to the long-term budgetary viability of the Platform, was pledging an additional €900,000 to the trust fund for 2024, bringing his Government’s total contribution for 2024 to €1 million. The representative of Belgium, reaffirming his Government’s strong support for the Platform and its objectives, announced a pledge of €66,000 to the trust fund for 2024. The representative of Japan, emphasizing the need for the Platform to operate in a sustainable manner and expressing concern that the estimated cumulative balance of its available funds would be exhausted by 2027, announced that his Government would contribute $189,814 for 2025 and would continue to provide in-kind and additional financial contributions for the technical support unit for the task force on scenarios and models of biodiversity and ecosystem services. The same representative expressed the hope that more member countries would contribute to the Platform’s funding, welcomed the secretariat’s fundraising efforts and highlighted that annual commitments should remain aligned with reliable income sources, as recommended following the review of IPBES at the conclusion of its first work programme.
The Plenary established a contact group on budget, chaired by Eric Grigoryan (Armenia), to consider further the financial and budgetary arrangements for the Platform.

Subsequently, the Chair of the contact group reported that the group had concluded its work on the financial and budgetary matters under discussion. He announced that an additional pledge of £50,000 for 2024 had been received from the Government of the United Kingdom.

The Plenary considered a draft decision on the matter. The Executive Secretary explained that the draft decision was missing an operative paragraph that had been approved by the contact group on budget. It would thus be updated to include that paragraph, in which the Executive Secretary was requested to explore options to reduce future budgetary deficits and to report thereon to the Plenary at its twelfth session.
The Plenary adopted decision IPBES-11/3, on financial and budgetary arrangements, as orally amended. The decision is set out in the annex to the present report.

division.heading: Assessing knowledge

subdivision.heading: Thematic assessment of the interlinkages among biodiversity, water, food and health

content.p: Introducing the sub-item, the Chair drew attention to the summary for policymakers of the thematic assessment of the interlinkages among biodiversity, water, food and health (IPBES/11/5), also known as the "nexus assessment"; the chapters of the thematic assessment (IPBES/11/INF/1); and the overview of the process followed for the preparation of the assessment (IPBES/11/INF/5). He thanked the Co-Chairs of the thematic assessment for their time and dedication over the previous four years and, through them, the many experts who had also contributed their time and effort.

The Plenary agreed to request working group I to consider the summary for policymakers, working on the basis of the Chair’s informal note on the matter and the proposed draft decision set out in document IPBES/11/1/Add.2. The working group was to be co-chaired by Bishwa Nath Oli (Nepal) and Douglas Beard (United States).

Subsequently, the Plenary considered the draft summary for policymakers of the thematic assessment of the interlinkages among biodiversity, water, food and health (the nexus assessment), which had been prepared by working group I, and a draft decision on the matter (IPBES/11/1/Add.2, section II), in which the Plenary would approve the summary for policymakers, as revised by the working group, and accept the chapters of the thematic assessment of the interlinkages among biodiversity, water, food and health (IPBES/11/INF/1), on the understanding that the chapters would be revised to duly reflect the revised summary.

In the ensuing discussion, the representative of the secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity emphasized the significance of the nexus assessment, highlighted the need for synergistic approaches to achieve the goals and targets of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and underscored the importance of taking into account the interlinkages between biodiversity, food, water and health, against the backdrop of a changing climate, in order to develop appropriate policy responses. Her secretariat, and in particular its Subsidiary Body on Scientific, Technical and Technological Advice, looked forward to incorporating the assessment into its processes and to future cooperation with the Platform.

The Co-Chairs of the nexus assessment delivered statements in which they reflected on the challenging process undertaken over several years to produce the assessment report, reaffirmed the importance of the nexus assessment to achieve the 2050 Vision for Biodiversity, and thanked all the stakeholders, authors, experts and technical support staff whose dedicated work, in the spirit of collaboration and cooperation, had enabled the production of a report that was very significant for the future of the planet.

The Plenary adopted decision IPBES-11/1 on the implementation of the rolling work programme of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services up to 2030, as orally amended, including part II thereof, entitled "Assessing knowledge", in which, among other things, it approved the summary for policymakers of the nexus assessment and accepted the chapters of the assessment, including their executive summaries. The decision is set out in the annex to the present report.

subdivision.heading: Thematic assessment of the underlying causes of biodiversity loss and the determinants of transformative change and options for achieving the 2050 Vision for Biodiversity

content.p: Introducing the sub-item, the Chair drew attention to the summary for policymakers of the thematic assessment of the underlying causes of biodiversity loss and the determinants of transformative change and options of achieving the 2050 Vision for Biodiversity (IPBES/11/6), also known as the "transformative change assessment"; the chapters of the thematic assessment (IPBES/11/INF/2); and the overview of the process followed for the preparation of the assessment (IPBES/11/INF/6). He thanked the Co-Chairs of the thematic assessment for their time and dedication over the past four years and, through them, the many experts who had also contributed much time and effort.

The Plenary agreed to request working group II to consider the summary for policymakers, working on the basis of the Chair’s informal note on the matter and the proposed draft decision set out in document IPBES/11/1/Add.2. The working group was to be co-chaired by Sebsebe Demissew (Ethiopia), Eeva Primmer (Finland) and Hesiquio Benítez Díaz (Mexico).

Subsequently, the Plenary considered the draft summary for policymakers of the thematic assessment of the underlying causes of biodiversity loss and the determinants of transformative change and options for achieving the 2050 Vision for Biodiversity (transformative change assessment), which had been prepared by the working group, and a draft decision on the matter, in which the Plenary would approve the summary for policymakers, as revised by the working group, and accept the chapters of the transformative change assessment (IPBES/11/INF/2), on the understanding that the chapters would be revised to duly reflect the revised summary.

One representative said that, as his delegation comprised only one person, he had not been able to participate in all the discussions of working group II on the matter. He had communicated that possibility to the Plenary on the first day of the session during the adoption of the agenda and had presented some general comments during the first meeting of the working group. However, while the efforts of the Co-Chairs of the working group to raise awareness of the concerns of his delegation were appreciated, the draft summary for policymakers that was before the Plenary had not adequately reflected those concerns. His delegation therefore intended to exercise its right to reopen the document to discuss proposed amendments that, in the opinion of his delegation, would add to the quality of the draft summary. He outlined the suggested amendments, indicating their priority, while highlighting the high regard held by his delegation for the work undertaken by the authors of the document and the Co-Chairs of the working group, and reassuring the Plenary that his delegation had no intention of blocking or impeding the approval by the Plenary of the draft summary for policymakers. Finally, he said that his proposed way forward was in keeping with rule 36, paragraph 1, of the rules of procedure for IPBES sessions, which stated that the members of the Platform took decisions on matters of substance by consensus, unless otherwise provided in its rules.

Several representatives opposed reopening the text for the purpose stated, for a number of reasons: the matter of small delegation size affected many parties and was not an undue hindrance to participation; it was important to place trust in the competencies of other team members when personal engagement did not prove possible; the draft summary for policymakers was strongly grounded in science and reflected the principles of scientific vigour and neutrality, and that scientific basis held priority over any personal textual preferences that may be put forward; the urgent priority attached to the transformative changes for achieving the 2050 Vision for Biodiversity set out in the summary for policymakers overrode any perceived need to seek incremental improvements that might delay its approval; and reopening text after its approval by a working group, following extensive negotiations to achieve a delicate balance of varied viewpoints, could set a precedent that could jeopardize the future smooth operation of the Platform.

Several representatives affirmed that delegates had the right to raise concerns and issues at any stage in the process of discussing and approving a draft summary for policymakers or similar matter. In addition, it was recognized that the representative who had proposed amendments had given due notice of his intention of doing so in Plenary. Several stressed the importance of the principles that underlay the work of the Platform, which included the principle of consensus, as set out in rule 36, paragraph 1, of the rules of procedure; deliberations on the present matter should move forward in accordance with those principles. One representative drew attention to paragraphs 3 and 4 of rule 36 of the rules of procedure, which offered guidance on how to move forward on matters where differing views were held.

Following the discussion, the representative who had proposed amendments said that he understood the concerns being raised by various representatives, but he reiterated that his party was exercising its legitimate right as a member to pursue the course of action proposed in order to improve the text of the document and to suggest amendments that would resonate with the national challenges of his country and of other developing countries. His party always engaged in negotiations in good faith and valued multilateralism and the principles of international law. The amendments he proposed would not undermine the scientific quality of the assessment and were based on a review of the literature informing the specific chapters for which textual changes were proposed.

The Chair convened a group of friends of the Chair, facilitated by Luthando Dziba, Co-Chair of the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel, to discuss the matter further. The group would comprise the representative who had proposed amendments, the Co-Chairs of working group II, coordinating lead authors of the summary for policymakers and representatives of other interested members.

Subsequently, the facilitator of the group of friends of the Chair reported that the group had reached agreement on a revised text of the summary for policymakers and he presented the proposed amendments to Plenary for its consideration.

The Plenary adopted decision IPBES-11/1, on the implementation of the rolling work programme of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services up to 2030, as orally amended, including part II thereof entitled "Assessing knowledge", in which, among other things, it approved the summary for policymakers of the thematic assessment of the underlying causes of biodiversity loss and the determinants of transformative change and options for achieving the 2050 Vision for Biodiversity (transformative change assessment), and accepted the chapters of the assessment, including their executive summaries. The decision is set out in the annex to the present report.

The representative of Brazil delivered a statement on matters of policy in line with paragraph 4 of rule 36 of the rules of procedure, requesting that the statement be reflected in the present report. He said that his country’s delegation to the meeting had consisted of a single delegate, posing a challenge to effective participation in both working groups taking place simultaneously. The text of the summary for policymakers should be read with due consideration to the difficulties faced by small delegations in actively presenting their views during negotiations. He emphasized that nothing in the document modified any of his country’s international legal obligations under the environmental and trade regimes. Moreover, the approval of the summary for policymakers and acceptance of the chapters did not imply that measures contained therein were consistent with relevant international obligations, in particular those under the World Trade Organization, and nothing in the summary for policymakers and the chapters of the assessment should be understood as an endorsement of any unilateral trade measures.

The Co-Chairs of the transformative change assessment delivered statements in which they reflected on the challenging process undertaken over several years to produce the assessment report; reaffirmed the importance of transformative change to achieve the 2050 Vision for Biodiversity; praised the dedication and spirit of compromise among all stakeholders that had enabled agreement on a science-policy document of huge significance to the future of the planet; reiterated that change must remain cognizant of the principles of equity, justice and respect for diversity; and thanked all the stakeholders, authors, experts and technical support staff whose dedicated work, within the spirit of collaboration and cooperation, had brought the present stage in the implementation of transformative change to its conclusion.

Several representatives made statements on the significance of the adoption of the summary for policymakers of the transformative change assessment and its importance to the continuing work on the science-policy interface, including under IPBES, and the importance of ensuring that policy was reflected in action.

One representative, speaking on behalf of a group of countries and asking that his remarks be reflected in the present report, expressed concern at the erosion of trust in the integrity of the science-policy platform that had been demonstrated at the current meeting, and asserted that the authors should be the first authority in explaining whether and how policy concerns could or could not be accommodated in the summary for policymakers. Lessons should be learned from the current session to avoid a similar situation in the future.

One representative, requesting that his remarks be reflected in the present report, made several observations: that the work accomplished at the current session exemplified the uniqueness of the IPBES process, which necessitated capacity-building for local focal points and delegates who were new to the process to allow them to fully understand the foundational principles of IPBES and enhance their contributions to its work; that it was important that full use be made of the rigorous multiple phases in the production of assessment reports, and that members participate in consultations and other preparatory work to maximize their contributions during Plenary sessions; that the summary for policymakers should be recognized as relevant to all countries, and it was therefore necessary to avoid redrafting the text based on individual national examples and experiences; and that the role of the authors, whose work was grounded in rigorously assessed evidence, should be respected.

subdivision.heading: Scoping report for a second global assessment of biodiversity and ecosystem services

content.p: Introducing the sub-item, the Chair drew attention to the scoping report for a second global assessment of biodiversity and ecosystem services (IPBES/11/7) and the overview of the process followed for the preparation of the scoping report (IPBES/11/INF/7). He expressed appreciation to the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel, the Bureau and the scoping experts who had contributed their time and effort to the report.

The Plenary agreed to request working group I to consider the scoping report, working on the basis of the Chair’s informal note on the matter and the proposed draft decision set out in document IPBES/11/1/Add.2.

The Plenary adopted decision IPBES-11/1 on the implementation of the rolling work programme of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services up to 2030, as orally amended, including part II thereof, entitled "Assessing knowledge", in which, among other things, it approved the undertaking of a second global assessment of biodiversity and ecosystem services, in accordance with the procedures for the preparation of Platform deliverables and as outlined in the scoping report for the assessment set out in annex I to the decision. The decision is set out in the annex to the present report.

subdivision.heading: Engagement with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change

content.p: Introducing the sub-item, the Chair drew attention to the note by the secretariat on engagement with IPCC (IPBES/11/8) and the compilation of further suggestions from members of IPBES regarding thematic or methodological issues related to biodiversity and climate change that would benefit from collaboration between IPCC and IPBES (IPBES/11/INF/10).

The Plenary agreed to request working group II to consider the proposed draft decision on the matter set out in document IPBES/11/1/Add.2, working on the basis of the Chair’s informal note on the matter.

The Plenary adopted decision IPBES-11/1 on the implementation of the rolling work programme of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services up to 2030, as orally amended, including part II thereof, entitled "Assessing knowledge", pertaining to, among other things, engagement with IPCC. The decision is set out in the annex to the present report.

At the time of the adoption, one representative noted that, during the informal consultations, his delegation had expressed concerns relating to the proposal to host an additional workshop. He trusted that the secretariat would ensure that the workshop mentioned in paragraph 14 of the draft decision was organized and convened in an inclusive and transparent manner in order to ensure the participation of all interested members, including with regard to geographical balance among the experts who would be invited.

division.heading: Building capacity, strengthening knowledge foundations and supporting policy

content.p: Introducing the item, the Chair drew attention to the note by the secretariat on work on building capacity, strengthening knowledge foundations and supporting policy (IPBES/11/9), in which workplans for the implementation of objectives 2, 3 and 4 of the rolling work programme up to 2030 were set out for the period between the eleventh and twelfth sessions, together with revised terms of reference for the task forces. Information on the work carried out by the task forces during the intersessional period preceding the current session was set out in documents IPBES/11/INF/13, IPBES/11/INF/14, IPBES/11/INF/15, IPBES/11/INF/16, IPBES/11/INF/17 and IPBES/11/INF/18.
He expressed appreciation to the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel, the Bureau and the task force members who had contributed to the work on those important functions.

The Plenary agreed to request working group II to consider the item, working on the basis of the Chair’s informal note on the matter and the proposed draft decision set out in document IPBES/11/1/Add.2.

Subsequently, the Plenary considered a draft decision on the matter. A representative of the secretariat, referring to part III of the draft decision, on "Building capacity", explained that operative paragraph 21, in which the Plenary approved the workplan for objective 2 of the work programme for the intersessional period, would be amended to include wording to the effect that the Plenary also approved indicators for measuring the workplan’s effectiveness.

The Plenary adopted decision IPBES-11/1 on the implementation of the rolling work programme of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services up to 2030, as orally amended, including parts III, IV, V and VII thereof, entitled "Building capacity", "Strengthening the knowledge foundations", "Supporting policy", and "Technical support for the work programme", respectively, pertaining to, among other things, the workplans of the attendant task forces for the intersessional period. The decision is set out in the annex to the present report.

division.heading: Improving the effectiveness of the Platform

content.p: Introducing the item, the Chair drew attention to the note by the secretariat on improving the effectiveness of the Platform (IPBES/11/10); an overview of responses by the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel, the Bureau and the Executive Secretary to the recommendations set out in the report on the review of the Platform at the end of its first work programme (IPBES/11/INF/21); and a report on the outcomes of the internal part of the midterm review of the Platform under the rolling work programme up to 2030 (IPBES/11/INF/22).
The Plenary agreed to request working group I to consider the item.
During its second meeting, in the light of the progress made in working groups I and II, the Plenary requested working group II to consider the item instead of working group I.

Subsequently, the Plenary adopted decision IPBES-11/1 on the implementation of the rolling work programme of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services up to 2030, as orally amended, including part VI thereof, entitled "Improving the effectiveness of the Platform". The decision is set out in the annex to the present report.

division.heading: Organization of the Plenary; dates and venues of future sessions of the Plenary

content.p: Introducing the item, the Chair drew attention to the information on the dates, venues and draft provisional agendas for the twelfth and thirteenth sessions of the Plenary set out in the note by the secretariat on the organization of work of the Plenary and dates and venues of future sessions of the Plenary (IPBES/11/11), noting that the Government of the United Kingdom had offered to host the twelfth session of IPBES.

The Chair invited Governments interested in hosting the thirteenth session of the Plenary to contact the secretariat as soon as possible so as to enable consideration of all offers at the current session.

Subsequently, the representative of the United Kingdom conveyed the offer by his Government to host the twelfth session of the Plenary in his country. He introduced a short video presentation highlighting that the country’s excellent centres of research and innovation and renowned institutions would provide a strong foundation for the launch of the business and biodiversity assessment. The Plenary gratefully accepted the offer.

One representative, welcoming the offer made by the Government of the United Kingdom, noted that London had the experience necessary to host large multilateral events. He expressed concern, however, that, owing to the visa requirements of the United Kingdom, many representatives might encounter difficulties in participating. His delegation was willing to join in the consensus on accepting the offer subject to the inclusion of an additional paragraph in the relevant draft decision in order to facilitate the approval of visas for representatives of all members. The representative noted that the proposed text was based on the guidelines for the preparation of host Government agreements falling under General Assembly resolution 40/243 and that it was standard wording in any host country agreement.

Welcoming the offer made by the Government of the United Kingdom, two representatives requested that free time be included in the schedule for the twelfth session in order to allow participants to experience the country and its beauty.

One representative encouraged the Bureau to consider alternative dates for the Plenary, possibly at another time of year, as a number of other environmental meetings were to be held towards the end of 2025, including the seventh session of the United Nations Environment Assembly. In addition, it was important to acknowledge that December was a challenging time of year for countries in the southern hemisphere, as it marked the beginning of summer there.
The Chair said that he would undertake informal consultations in relation to the draft decision on the item.

Subsequently, the Plenary considered a draft decision on the matter. The Plenary adopted decision IPBES-11/2 on the organization of the Plenary and dates and venues of future sessions of the Plenary. The decision is set out in the annex to the present report.

The representative of the United Kingdom, welcoming the Plenary’s support for the offer by his Government to host the twelfth session of the Plenary, emphasized that the feedback concerning the dates of the next Plenary would be taken into account and that efforts would be made to avoid clashes with other intergovernmental meetings and to ensure the full, effective and meaningful participation of all.

division.heading: Institutional arrangements: United Nations collaborative partnership arrangement for the work of the Platform and its secretariat

content.p: Introducing the item, the Chair recalled that, in its decision IPBES-2/8, the Plenary had approved a collaborative partnership arrangement to establish an institutional link between the Plenary of the Platform and UNEP, UNESCO, FAO and UNDP, as set out in the annex to the decision.

A representative of UNESCO, speaking on behalf of the four United Nations system partners of IPBES, presented the progress report on the United Nations collaborative partnership arrangement (IPBES/11/INF/23).
The Chair expressed his appreciation to UNEP, UNESCO, FAO and UNDP for the support they had provided to the Platform and asked them to continue to provide such support throughout the work programme.

division.heading: Adoption of the decisions and the report of the session

content.p: The Plenary adopted decisions IPBES-11/1–IPBES-11/3, as set out in the annex to the present report.

The Plenary adopted the present report on the basis of the draft report that had been circulated, on the understanding that the report would be finalized by the secretariat under the supervision of the Bureau.

division.heading: Closure of the session

content.p: On the closing day of the session, several representatives, speaking on behalf of the IPBES family, paid tribute to Ms. Larigauderie, who was stepping down as Executive Secretary of the Platform. Mr. Beard, a Bureau member, Mr. Dziba, Co-Chair of the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel, and Ms. Ruth Spencer, a representative of local communities from Antigua and Barbuda, all praised Ms. Larigauderie for her leadership, energy and commitment to excellence and acknowledged the many accomplishments of the Plenary under her direction. Polina Shulbaeva, a representative of the International Indigenous Forum on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services, also presented the Executive Secretary with a piece of art by an Indigenous artist from Namibia.

Ms. Larigauderie expressed gratitude for the kind comments and the trust that had been placed in her. She wished the Plenary the strength and courage to continue a collective job which, she said, was far from done, as there would always be a need for science and knowledge of nature to inform decision-making.
Following the customary exchange of courtesies, the Chair declared the session closed at 10.40 p.m. on 16 December 2024.

subdivision.heading: Scope and rationale

content.p:
The overall objective of the second Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) global assessment of biodiversity and ecosystem services (referred to hereafter as "the second global assessment") is to assess relevant knowledge that has become available since the publication of The Global Assessment Report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
IPBES (2019). The Global Assessment Report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services. Brondizio, E. S., Settele, J., Díaz, S. and Ngo, H. T. (eds.). IPBES secretariat, Bonn, Germany. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3831673. and assess progress towards achieving the goals of sustainability and living in harmony with nature. The second global assessment will strengthen the science-policy interface on biodiversity and nature’s contributions to people on a range of spatial scales, from the local to the global, by providing the knowledge and the policy support tools needed for informed decision-making. The second global assessment will be delivered in 2028.

intro.p: The specific objectives of the second global assessment are:

content.p: To support Governments and other actors in implementing the objectives of relevant multilateral environmental agreements and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its Sustainable Development Goals;

To support the assessment of progress towards the achievement of the global targets for 2030 and the global goals for 2050 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework
Adopted by the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity in decision 15/4. and of relevant Sustainable Development Goals and targets;

To assess the scientific and technical basis as well as different knowledge systems and policy-relevant information for the additional efforts needed in the current and subsequent decades to achieve the 2050 Vision for Biodiversity.

Prior assessments have highlighted the multiple direct and underlying drivers that are leading to the decline of nature; complex and intersecting response pathways; and the essential role of justice and equity in transforming societal actions across the planet to halt and reverse the decline of nature and to increase nature’s contributions to people. The second global assessment will build on these findings by critically reviewing new evidence relating to the status and trends of the loss of biodiversity and nature’s contributions to people, the causation in relation to multiple drivers, and the consequences for people and nature. It will evaluate new information on the urgency of action and consequences of delayed action, and on the experiences of effecting transformative change and further options for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals and the vision of living in harmony with nature.

The second global assessment will incorporate and build on completed IPBES assessments and the findings of other science-policy panels, identifying policy-relevant information for achieving the global goals referred to in paragraph 2 above. Countries have faced immense challenges in achieving some of the objectives and targets agreed to date. The second global assessment will reflect on these challenges and also highlight positive examples, showing enabling conditions for success and indicating ways to address challenges and barriers so that successful and effective approaches could be extended and replicated on a variety of scales to add up to the desired outcomes at the global scale outlined in paragraph 2.

It will also address critical gaps in the first Global Assessment as well as emerging issues. These gaps and issues include the need for more comprehensive attention to oceans. It will also consider neglected components of biodiversity; multiple world views and different knowledge systems; and relevant social issues and different social groups. The second global assessment will assess the different challenges, lessons learned and potential solutions within and among regions in a scientific and balanced manner. The issues related to Indigenous Peoples and local communities will be comprehensively addressed, including multiple world views and values.

The second global assessment will highlight and synthesize the findings of prior assessments relating to the differing roles of actors such as Governments, Indigenous Peoples and local communities, the private sector and civil society, women and youth, and their value systems, in delivering the building blocks for transformative change. A dedicated chapter on multiple knowledge systems, with a focus on Indigenous and local knowledge, will provide for greater inclusion, introducing content that will be woven through all the chapters of the assessment. Consistent with all IPBES assessments, the second global assessment will provide a technically and scientifically balanced evaluation of global biodiversity and ecosystem services being scientifically independent and unbiased as well as remaining neutral with respect to policy.

The second global assessment will cover both regional and global dimensions. It will provide information relevant to all biogeographic and oceanographic zones from the regional to the global level, including terrestrial, inland water, coastal and marine ecosystems.

In line with the monitoring framework for the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the assessment will prioritize the period 2011–2020 as the reference period for monitoring and reporting progress.

The analyses will consider trends up to 2025, focusing primarily on the past 50 years and, where information is available, looking back prior to the industrial revolution or as far back as is clearly relevant. The analyses will also consider future pathways up to 2100, or as far forward as relevant, with a focus on the period 2030–2050. Long-term historical data will be used as an information source for possible baselines and contemporary reference states that could be considered for various national, regional or global indicator comparisons.

The assessment will consist of a summary for policymakers and five chapters, each with an executive summary of the key findings of that chapter. The assessment will also include a cross-chapter synthesis of the findings on oceans. The length of the summary for policymakers should remain within a limit of approximately 10,000 words. Indicative word limits are also provided in the chapter outline below.

The assessment will apply the IPBES conceptual framework.
